question: Six Scrum Teams are building one product together. How many Product Backlogs should exist?
options: One per Scrum Team, consolidated by the Product Owner before each Sprint
One per Scrum Team, plus a master backlog maintained by a program manager
Two: one for features and one for technical work, split across the teams
One Product Backlog for the product, shared by all six teams
explanation: Scrum states that multiple teams working on one product share one Product Backlog, one Product Owner and one Product Goal. Team-specific backlogs or a separate technical backlog fragment ordering and make overall value optimization impossible. A 'master backlog' owned by a program manager would remove accountability from the Product Owner.

question: An organization is adding a second and third Scrum Team to an existing product. Which elements must remain singular across all three teams? (Choose two.)
options: One Scrum Master shared by all three teams
One Product Owner accountable for maximizing the product's value
One Sprint length identical for every team in the organization
One Product Backlog with a single ordering
One Daily Scrum attended by all three teams together
explanation: For a single product, Scrum requires one Product Owner and one Product Backlog so value can be optimized across all the work. A Scrum Master may serve more than one team but this is not required, synchronized Sprint lengths are a common convenience rather than a rule, and a joint Daily Scrum would defeat the event's purpose for each Developer group.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Owner / Product Backlog

question: Four teams on the same product each produce their own Increment and integration happens in a separate 'integration Sprint' every quarter. What is the most important problem with this arrangement?
options: The teams should have four Definitions of Done so each can optimize locally
The Scrum Masters should take over the integration work themselves
Quarterly integration is acceptable as long as the Product Owner approves it
Integration risk and defects accumulate invisibly, so no usable integrated Increment exists at the end of each Sprint
explanation: Multiple teams on one product must produce a single integrated Increment that meets the Definition of Done by the end of each Sprint, otherwise empiricism breaks down because no one can inspect the real state of the product. Deferred integration hides defects and creates unpredictable rework. Local Definitions of Done and Scrum Masters doing the work would make the dysfunction worse.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Increment / Definition of Done

question: Three teams on one product use different Definitions of Done, with one team excluding performance testing. What should the Scrum Master encourage?
options: Each team keeping its own Definition of Done since teams are self-managing
The Product Owner deciding on behalf of the teams which tests are mandatory
Postponing performance testing to a dedicated hardening Sprint before release
The teams agreeing on a common Definition of Done that all of them apply, each team being free to make it stricter for its own work
explanation: When multiple teams work on the same product they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done; individual teams may apply stricter criteria but never weaker ones. Self-management does not permit releasing an Increment of inconsistent quality. Hardening Sprints push quality work out of the Sprint and are an anti-pattern.

question: How many Product Goals can a single product have active at one time in Scrum?
options: One Product Goal at a time; the Scrum Team fulfills or abandons it before taking the next
One per Scrum Team working on the product
As many as the stakeholders request each quarter
One per Sprint, created during Sprint Planning
explanation: The Product Goal describes the future state of the product and a Scrum Team must fulfill or abandon one Product Goal before taking on the next. A per-Sprint objective is the Sprint Goal, not the Product Goal. Teams sharing a product share the same Product Goal.

question: A manager proposes organizing five teams on one product by technical layer: a UI team, a services team and a database team. Why is this a concern for a Scrum Master?
options: Component teams cannot deliver a done, valuable slice of product alone, creating dependencies and handoffs that delay value
Scrum forbids any form of specialization among Developers
Component teams make it impossible to hold a Sprint Retrospective
It would require five Product Owners instead of one
explanation: Component teams each own a technical layer, so delivering any user-facing capability requires coordinating multiple teams, which creates handoffs, queues and partial Increments. Scrum does not forbid specialists, it requires the team collectively to have all skills to create a done Increment each Sprint. Retrospectives are still possible, they just surface the dependency pain.

question: Three teams share one Product Backlog. Each Sprint, several items turn out to need work from two teams, causing delays. What is the most effective long-term response?
options: Appoint a dependency manager to schedule cross-team work in advance
Have the Product Owner order the backlog so that each team only ever gets independent items
Add a two-week buffer Sprint after every three Sprints to absorb delays
Help the teams reduce dependencies by broadening skills and reshaping team boundaries around end-to-end value, while coordinating openly in the meantime
explanation: The durable fix is to lower the structural need for coordination by forming teams that can deliver end-to-end slices and by spreading skills, while using transparent cross-team coordination for remaining dependencies. A dependency manager and buffer Sprints institutionalize the problem instead of removing it. Ordering the backlog purely to avoid dependencies would subordinate value to team structure.

question: Which statements about Sprint Reviews when several teams build one product are consistent with Scrum? (Choose two.)
options: The Sprint Review is a formal sign-off gate where stakeholders approve the release
The Product Backlog may be adjusted as a result of the discussion
Stakeholders inspect the integrated Increment and collaborate on what to do next
Each team should review only its own partial output with its own stakeholders
Only the Product Owner may speak to stakeholders during the event
explanation: The Sprint Review is a working session in which the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome and adapt the Product Backlog based on what was learned, and with multiple teams the object of inspection is the integrated Increment. It is not a sign-off gate, reviewing only partial outputs hides integration reality, and the whole Scrum Team collaborates with stakeholders.

question: A Product Owner responsible for eight teams cannot keep the Product Backlog ordered and is becoming a bottleneck. Which option best preserves Scrum's accountabilities?
options: Split the product into eight products with eight Product Owners regardless of how coupled they are
Let each Scrum Master order the portion of the backlog their team will work on
Create a committee that votes on Product Backlog order each Sprint
Keep one Product Owner accountable, while they delegate backlog refinement work and bring in people to help, and consider whether the product definition is too broad
explanation: The Product Owner remains a single accountable person but may have others do backlog work on their behalf, and an overloaded Product Owner is a signal to re-examine how the product is defined. Committees and Scrum Masters ordering work destroy the single point of accountability. Arbitrarily splitting a coupled product creates dependencies and sub-optimized value.

question: An organization adopts a scaling framework and immediately adds release trains, architecture boards and quarterly planning events. Developers report that nothing is delivered any faster. What should the Scrum Master emphasize first?
options: That the scaling framework must be followed more rigorously before results appear
That the organization should return to a single team and abandon the product
That scaling frameworks are mandated by the Scrum Guide and must be configured correctly
That the fundamental constraint is the ability to produce a done, integrated Increment each Sprint, and added process layers do not remove that constraint
explanation: Scaling adds coordination overhead but does not solve the underlying need for teams to deliver an integrated, done Increment every Sprint, which is where flow is usually blocked. Scrum itself does not mandate any scaling framework. Adding more ceremony or abandoning the product avoids addressing the real impediment, often technical and organizational.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Increment / Professional Scrum competencies

question: Who is responsible for inviting the right stakeholders to the Sprint Review?
options: The Scrum Master, as the organizer of all events
The project management office
The Developers, since they demonstrate the work
The Product Owner, who manages stakeholder collaboration for the product
explanation: The Product Owner represents the needs of stakeholders and is accountable for engaging the people whose feedback matters for the product. The Scrum Master helps the event be effective and may coach the Product Owner, but does not own stakeholder relationships. Scrum has no PMO accountability.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Owner / Sprint Review

question: Stakeholders repeatedly approach Developers mid-Sprint with urgent requests. What is the best action by the Scrum Master?
options: Instruct the Developers to accept any request from senior stakeholders
Block all stakeholder contact with the Developers permanently
Add all requests to the current Sprint Backlog so stakeholders feel heard
Help stakeholders understand that scope changes flow through the Product Owner, and that the Sprint Goal protects focus, while keeping open collaboration
explanation: Only the Product Owner can change the Product Backlog and no change may endanger the Sprint Goal, so the Scrum Master coaches stakeholders toward the right channel without isolating the team. Accepting every request destroys focus, while an absolute communication ban removes valuable collaboration. Silently absorbing all requests undermines the Sprint Goal.

question: A business analyst acts as 'Product Owner' but must get every decision approved by a steering committee that meets monthly. What is the key dysfunction?
options: The Product Owner is a proxy without the authority to decide, so backlog decisions are slow and the team cannot inspect and adapt quickly
Scrum forbids steering committees of any kind in an organization
A business analyst can never fulfill the Product Owner accountability
The team needs a second Product Owner to speed up approvals
explanation: For a Product Owner to succeed the whole organization must respect their decisions, and a proxy who cannot decide reintroduces delay and hand-offs that undermine empiricism. Scrum does not ban governance bodies, but it does require decision authority to rest with one person. A person's job title does not disqualify them; lack of authority does.

question: Which actions help a Scrum Master serve the organization in adopting Scrum? (Choose three.)
options: Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization
Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams
Assigning Product Backlog items to individual Developers
Approving which features the Product Owner releases
Leading, training and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption
explanation: The Scrum Master serves the organization by leading and coaching the adoption, planning and advising implementations, and removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams. Release decisions belong to the Product Owner, and the Developers themselves decide who does which work in the Sprint Backlog.

question: Executives ask for a monthly status report showing percentage completion per team. How should the Scrum Master respond?
options: Refuse, because reporting is forbidden in Scrum
Delegate the report to the Developers so the Product Owner is not disturbed
Produce the report personally each month so the team is left alone
Explore what decisions the executives need to make, and offer transparency based on working Increments and actual outcomes rather than percentage complete
explanation: The Scrum Master serves the organization by helping stakeholders get the transparency they need, and a done Increment is a far more honest signal than an estimate of percentage complete. Scrum does not forbid reporting, but it discourages measures that create false confidence. Quietly producing reports makes the Scrum Master a secretary rather than a change agent.

question: Which description best fits stakeholders in Scrum?
options: Members of the Scrum Team who do not write code
Anyone who attends the Daily Scrum to monitor progress
Managers who approve the Sprint Backlog before the Sprint begins
People outside the Scrum Team with a valid interest in the product who collaborate most closely at the Sprint Review
explanation: Stakeholders are people outside the Scrum Team who have an interest in the product, and the Sprint Review is the formal opportunity for them to inspect the Increment and collaborate on next steps. No one approves the Sprint Backlog, which belongs to the Developers. The Daily Scrum is for the Developers.

question: A Scrum Team's stakeholders never attend the Sprint Review, saying they are too busy. What is the best first step?
options: Cancel the Sprint Review until attendance improves
Escalate to HR to make attendance mandatory
Replace the Sprint Review with a written status email
Help the Product Owner understand why stakeholders see no value in attending and make the event worth their time by inspecting real working functionality and real outcomes
explanation: Low attendance is a symptom, usually that the event feels like a demo of little relevance or that the Increment is not truly usable; making the event valuable is the Scrum Master's coaching opportunity. The Sprint Review is a required event and cannot simply be cancelled or downgraded to email. Coercion rarely produces genuine collaboration.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Sprint Review / Scrum Master

question: After six months of Scrum, a company still releases only twice a year because of a separate change advisory board and a manual regression cycle. How should the Scrum Master treat this?
options: As acceptable, because Scrum only requires a potentially releasable Increment, not a release
As a problem for the Developers to solve alone during the Sprint Retrospective
As a reason to lengthen Sprints to six months to match the release cadence
As an organizational impediment to be made transparent and worked on with leadership, since the delay prevents feedback and value delivery
explanation: While Scrum does not force a release every Sprint, a release constraint of this size blocks empirical feedback and value, so making it transparent and coaching leadership is core Scrum Master work for the organization. Lengthening Sprints reduces feedback further. Such systemic constraints are beyond what the Developers alone can fix.

question: A Scrum Master notices they spend most of their week booking rooms, updating the task board for others and taking meeting minutes. Which statements are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: The Scrum Master is accountable for the team's effectiveness and should focus on coaching, impediment removal and organizational change
This is the Scrum Master as secretary anti-pattern and limits their true contribution
Scrum requires the Scrum Master to record minutes of every event
Administrative tasks are the core of the Scrum Master accountability
The Scrum Master must maintain the Sprint Backlog because the Developers are too busy
explanation: The Scrum Master is a true leader accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness, serving through coaching, facilitation, impediment removal and organizational change, not clerical work. The Sprint Backlog is owned and updated by the Developers, and Scrum prescribes no minutes.

question: A Scrum Master identifies an impediment that requires changing a company-wide procurement policy. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Make the impact transparent with evidence, engage the people who own the policy, and coach for change while helping the team cope in the meantime
Instruct the Developers to bypass the policy quietly
Ignore it, since only team-level impediments are in scope
Wait until an executive notices the problem on their own
explanation: Scrum Masters serve the organization and cause the removal of impediments, which often means influencing people they do not manage by making the cost visible and collaborating on change. Ignoring systemic impediments abandons a core part of the accountability. Bypassing policy secretly destroys trust and transparency.

question: A functional manager insists on attending the Daily Scrum and asking each Developer for a status update. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Allow it, because managers must be kept informed daily
Ask the Product Owner to run the Daily Scrum instead so the manager speaks to them
Cancel the Daily Scrum while the manager is interested in attending
Coach the manager on the purpose of the event and help them find other ways to get the information, ensuring the Daily Scrum stays the Developers' planning session
explanation: The Daily Scrum is for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan; turning it into a status report to a manager undermines self-management. The Scrum Master coaches those involved so the event keeps its purpose and finds other transparency channels. Cancelling the event or reassigning facilitation does not address the behavior.

question: In Scrum, who is accountable for removing impediments that block the Developers' progress?
options: The Scrum Master, who causes their removal
The project manager assigned to the team
The Product Owner, who sets priorities
The most senior Developer
explanation: The Scrum Master serves the Scrum Team by causing the removal of impediments to its progress, which may mean resolving them directly or enabling others to do so. Scrum defines no project manager accountability. The Product Owner focuses on value and the Product Backlog.

question: Leadership asks a Scrum Master to prove that the Scrum adoption is working. Which indicators give the most meaningful evidence? (Choose two.)
options: Time from idea to value delivered to a customer
Number of Scrum events held per Sprint
Average velocity increase across all teams
Frequency with which usable Increments reach users and the resulting customer outcomes
Percentage of Developers certified in Scrum
explanation: Evidence-based thinking focuses on value actually realized and on the ability to deliver, such as delivery frequency, customer outcomes and time to market, rather than on activity or output measures. Velocity is not part of Scrum and rises trivially by inflating estimates. Event counts and certifications measure compliance, not value.

question: A Scrum Master is told by a director: 'Just make the teams follow the process; the organizational issues are not your concern.' What is the most professional response?
options: Explain, with concrete examples, how organizational constraints limit the teams' ability to deliver value, and offer to work with leadership on them
Resign from the accountability immediately
Comply, focusing only on event attendance and board hygiene
Escalate anonymously to the company's board of directors
explanation: Serving the organization is an explicit part of the Scrum Master accountability, and the professional approach is to make the cost of the constraints transparent and invite collaboration. Policing process compliance produces mechanical Scrum without benefit. Anonymous escalation or quitting at the first disagreement forgoes the chance to influence change.

question: Two Scrum Teams on one product disagree about an architectural approach and the dispute is delaying work. What is the most appropriate Scrum Master behavior?
options: Decide the architecture personally to end the dispute
Escalate to the enterprise architecture board for a binding ruling
Ask the Product Owner to choose the technical design
Facilitate a conversation where both teams make their reasoning and constraints transparent and converge on a decision they will test empirically
explanation: Developers are accountable for technical decisions, and the Scrum Master's role is to facilitate the conversation so a decision emerges and can be validated by building something. Deciding for them or handing the choice to the Product Owner removes self-management and technical accountability. External rulings may be slow and uninformed by the teams' direct experience.

question: What is the main difference between Scrum and traditional predictive project management regarding plans?
options: Scrum replans continuously based on empirical evidence from working Increments, rather than following a detailed upfront plan
Scrum plans only once, at the start of the product
Scrum has no plans at all
Scrum plans in more detail upfront than waterfall but reviews it less often
explanation: Scrum is founded on empiricism: decisions are based on what is observed, and the plan is adapted every Sprint, every Daily Scrum and at the Sprint Review. Scrum has plans at several levels, including the Sprint Backlog and the Product Backlog. Detailed upfront plans in complex work tend to be wrong rather than a source of control.

question: A customer insists on a fixed scope, fixed date and fixed price contract for a complex product. Which approach best fits empirical delivery?
options: Promise the full scope and manage change requests through a formal change control board
Estimate the whole backlog in detail first, then add a 40 percent buffer to be safe
Decline all contracts that mention a budget
Fix the budget and date while keeping scope variable and ordered by value, delivering the most valuable items first and letting the customer steer each Sprint
explanation: In complex work the realistic contract shape fixes time and money and varies scope, so the customer can continuously re-order remaining work and stop when enough value is delivered. Fixing everything and relabelling inevitable change as exceptions does not reduce uncertainty. Large upfront estimates with buffers give false precision and lock in waste.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Empiricism / Professional Scrum competencies

question: Which statements about forecasting in Scrum are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A forecast fixes the Product Backlog for the rest of the release
The Product Owner must guarantee the forecast to stakeholders
A forecast is a probabilistic projection based on past empirical data, not a commitment
Forecast accuracy improves as more is learned and remaining work decreases
Scrum prescribes burndown charts as the forecasting tool
explanation: Scrum Teams use past performance to project likely future progress, and such forecasts become more reliable as uncertainty is reduced, but they are never guarantees. The only commitment to deliver within a Sprint is the Sprint Goal, not a long-range forecast. Burndowns and similar charts are useful complementary practices, not Scrum elements.

question: A sponsor demands a precise date for delivery of 180 Product Backlog items. The team has completed three Sprints. What is the most honest and useful response?
options: Offer a range of likely completion dates based on observed delivery so far, explain the assumptions, and commit to updating it every Sprint
Refuse to say anything about dates because Scrum does not predict the future
Give a single date derived from average velocity, since three Sprints is enough data
Promise the date the sponsor wants and manage scope quietly later
explanation: Empiricism supports projecting a range with explicit assumptions and refreshing it as evidence accumulates, which gives the sponsor a basis for decisions without false precision. A single-point date from three data points conveys more certainty than the data supports. Silence is unhelpful and quiet scope manipulation destroys trust and transparency.

question: Management compares two Scrum Teams by their velocity and rewards the one with the higher number. What is the primary problem?
options: Velocity is an official Scrum metric that must only be reported to the Product Owner
Velocity should be measured in hours instead of points to be comparable
Velocity should be compared only across teams of the same size
Velocity numbers are team-relative and not comparable, and incentivizing them drives estimate inflation rather than value
explanation: Velocity is not part of Scrum; where used it is a team-internal planning aid based on that team's own relative estimates, so cross-team comparison is meaningless. Making it a performance target predictably inflates estimates and reduces quality. Changing the unit does not make team-relative estimates comparable.

question: Which statement about velocity is accurate with respect to the Scrum Guide 2020?
options: Velocity is not defined in the Scrum Guide; it is an optional complementary practice some teams use to help with forecasting
Velocity must be approved by the Product Owner before Sprint Planning
Velocity is a mandatory Scrum artifact measured each Sprint
Velocity replaces the Sprint Goal as the Sprint commitment
explanation: The Scrum Guide 2020 does not mention velocity, story points or burndown charts; they are complementary practices teams may adopt. The commitment for the Sprint Backlog is the Sprint Goal. Nothing about velocity requires Product Owner approval.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Scrum Theory / complementary practices

question: A team's velocity dropped sharply for two Sprints after they added automated testing to their Definition of Done. How should the Scrum Master frame this to management?
options: As a performance problem that requires replacing team members
As irrelevant, since velocity should never be discussed
As a reason to remove the automated testing from the Definition of Done
As a predictable short-term effect of raising quality, which reduces rework and improves sustainable delivery and predictability over time
explanation: Strengthening the Definition of Done means more work is done per item, so a short-term output dip is expected while defect rates and rework fall, improving flow and predictability. Reverting the Definition of Done trades long-term capability for a vanity number. Treating it as a people problem misreads the cause.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Definition of Done / Increment

question: During release planning, a Product Owner must choose between two sets of Product Backlog items of similar cost. Which basis for the decision best reflects evidence-based thinking?
options: The expected outcome and value for customers and the business, including the information each option would reveal
The number of story points each set represents
Which set was requested by the most senior stakeholder
Which set the Developers find technically more interesting
explanation: Value is measured by outcomes for customers and the business, and in complex work the learning an option generates is itself valuable. Story point totals describe effort, not worth. Seniority of the requester and developer preference are not measures of value.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Owner / Evidence-Based Management

question: Which practices help a Product Owner manage a budget empirically on a long-running product? (Choose two.)
options: Delivering the most valuable items first so that stopping at any point leaves maximum value delivered
Allocating a fixed share of each Sprint's budget to each stakeholder group
Requiring all Product Backlog items to be estimated in hours before funding
Funding the product incrementally and re-deciding continuation based on delivered value
Committing the full multi-year budget to a fixed scope upfront
explanation: Incremental funding plus value-ordered delivery lets the organization capture value early and stop or redirect spend when returns fall, which matches empirical process control. Locking a multi-year budget to fixed scope assumes predictability that does not exist in complex work. Hour-based estimates of everything and per-stakeholder quotas optimize for the illusion of control or fairness rather than value.

question: A vendor and customer sign a time-and-materials contract with a Scrum Team. The customer worries about getting value for money. Which mechanism in Scrum most directly addresses that worry?
options: Detailed weekly timesheets reviewed by the customer
A penalty clause tied to velocity targets
A frequent, usable Increment inspected at every Sprint Review, letting the customer judge value and steer or stop at short intervals
A signed requirements specification baselined before the first Sprint
explanation: Delivering a usable Increment each Sprint gives the customer real evidence of progress and the option to redirect or terminate with little exposure, which is stronger protection than paperwork. Timesheets measure effort, not value. Velocity penalties invite gaming and a baselined specification removes the ability to adapt.

question: A traditional project manager asks who in Scrum is responsible for the project's schedule, scope and cost tracking. What is the best answer?
options: Those concerns are distributed: the Product Owner manages value and the Product Backlog, the Developers manage how work is done each Sprint, and the Scrum Team inspects and adapts every Sprint
The Scrum Master, who acts as the project manager
No one; Scrum does not care about cost or scope
A project management office that oversees the Scrum Team
explanation: Scrum has no project manager; the accountabilities traditionally bundled into that role are distributed across the Product Owner, the Developers and the whole Scrum Team, with the Sprint cadence providing control. Scrum does care about cost and scope, but manages them empirically. The Scrum Master is not a project manager in disguise.

question: Why does Scrum favor short Sprints in environments of high uncertainty?
options: Because they reduce the cost of the Scrum events
Because management can reassign Developers more often
Because they let the team avoid writing a Sprint Goal
Because they generate more frequent opportunities to inspect and adapt, limiting risk to the cost of one Sprint
explanation: Shorter Sprints produce more learning cycles and cap the risk of going in a wrong direction to one Sprint's cost. Events are proportionally time-boxed, so shorter Sprints do not avoid them. Every Sprint still needs a Sprint Goal, and stable teams remain important.

question: A team is asked to produce a detailed, task-level plan for the next six Sprints before work starts. What is the strongest argument against this?
options: Planning is forbidden outside Sprint Planning
The Developers do not have time to plan
In complex work most of the detail will be invalidated by what is learned, so the effort creates waste and a false sense of control; detail is best added just in time
Only the Product Owner is allowed to plan beyond the current Sprint
explanation: Empiricism assumes that knowledge emerges, so detailed long-range task plans decay quickly and the effort spent is largely wasted while encouraging unwarranted confidence. Scrum does allow longer-range planning, but at a level of detail proportional to certainty. Refinement across Sprints is a collaborative activity, not restricted to the Product Owner.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Empiricism / Product Backlog refinement

question: A Product Owner wants to know when a specific feature set will be ready. Which practice best supports an empirical answer?
options: Using observed delivery data from recent Sprints together with the ordered Product Backlog to project a range, and revising it each Sprint
Asking each Developer for a personal estimate in hours and summing them
Dividing total remaining story points by the highest velocity achieved so far
Having the Scrum Master calculate the date from the original project plan
explanation: Projections based on actual recent throughput plus the current backlog order give an evidence-based range that is updated as reality changes. Using the best-ever velocity produces an optimistic single date. Hour summation ignores the emergent nature of the work, and the Scrum Master does not own forecasting.

question: Halfway through a funded release, measurements show that delivered features are barely used by customers. What should the Product Owner most likely do?
options: Continue as planned because the budget was approved for the full release
Wait until the release is complete before evaluating usage
Ask the Developers to increase velocity to finish the release sooner
Use the evidence to re-order or abandon remaining items and pursue a more valuable direction, possibly reconsidering the Product Goal
explanation: Outcome evidence is exactly what should drive adaptation of the Product Backlog and, if needed, the Product Goal; completing a plan that is not producing value wastes the remaining budget. Faster delivery of unused features increases waste rather than value. Deferring evaluation discards the advantage of frequent feedback.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Owner / Product Goal

question: Which are legitimate uses of a team's historical delivery data? (Choose two.)
options: Comparing teams to decide which gets more funding
Informing a range-based release forecast for stakeholders
Helping the Developers judge how much they can take on in Sprint Planning
Proving to auditors that the team is working hard enough
Setting individual performance targets for each Developer
explanation: Past performance helps a team size its own Sprint plan and helps the Product Owner project a realistic range for longer-term delivery. Using the same data for individual targets, cross-team funding decisions or effort policing turns a planning aid into a control mechanism that distorts behavior.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Sprint Planning / complementary practices

question: Which statement best contrasts the handling of change in Scrum with traditional change control?
options: Scrum treats change as expected and incorporates it through continuous Product Backlog refinement and re-ordering, protecting only the current Sprint Goal
Scrum prevents change during a release to protect the plan
Scrum requires a change request form for every new Product Backlog item
Scrum allows any change at any time, including changes to the current Sprint Goal
explanation: In Scrum new information continuously updates the Product Backlog, while the Sprint Goal remains stable so the Developers can focus for the Sprint. Scrum does not use change request bureaucracy, and the Sprint Goal is not altered mid-Sprint, though scope within the Sprint can be renegotiated.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - The Sprint / Product Backlog

question: What is the commitment associated with the Product Backlog?
options: The Sprint Goal
The Definition of Done
The Product Goal
The release plan
explanation: Each artifact has a commitment: the Product Backlog has the Product Goal, the Sprint Backlog has the Sprint Goal, and the Increment has the Definition of Done. A release plan is not a Scrum element.

question: A programme office wants Scrum Teams to report the variance between planned and actual story points each Sprint. What is the most useful coaching point?
options: Estimate variance is the best measure of team maturity
Teams should pad estimates so that variance is always near zero
Variance against estimates measures prediction accuracy, not value; focusing on delivered outcomes and the ability to meet Sprint Goals is more informative
Story points should be converted to hours to reduce variance
explanation: Chasing low estimate variance rewards padding and conservative behavior rather than value delivery, whereas Sprint Goal achievement and customer outcomes reflect real effectiveness. Estimates are an aid, not a contract. Converting units does not change what is being measured.

question: A fixed-date regulatory deadline cannot move and the full desired scope will not fit. Which approach is most consistent with Scrum?
options: Extend Sprints to reduce overhead and fit more work
Lower the Definition of Done temporarily so more items can be marked complete
Order the Product Backlog so the mandatory regulatory capability is delivered and validated first, then use remaining capacity for the next most valuable items
Add more teams in the final month to accelerate
explanation: With a fixed date the variable is scope, so delivering and validating the mandatory capability earliest removes the greatest risk. Weakening the Definition of Done creates undone work and hidden risk rather than progress. Longer Sprints reduce feedback and late staffing additions typically slow a team further.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Backlog / Definition of Done

question: Which of the following are anti-patterns when applying Scrum? (Choose three.)
options: Treating the Scrum Master as the person who writes all status reports
Refining Product Backlog items during the Sprint so upcoming work is understood
A Sprint Zero used to produce architecture and plans before any Increment
The Developers deciding among themselves how to turn backlog items into an Increment
A hardening Sprint at the end of a release to fix defects and finish testing
explanation: Sprint Zero, hardening Sprints and the Scrum Master as reporter all contradict Scrum: every Sprint must produce a usable Increment, quality work belongs inside the Sprint via the Definition of Done, and the Scrum Master is a leader not a clerk. Ongoing refinement and Developer self-management are proper Scrum behaviors.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - The Sprint / Scrum Master

question: Stakeholders ask why the Scrum Team will not promise a precise delivery date for a new, unprecedented product. Which explanation is best?
options: Because Scrum Teams are not allowed to discuss dates with stakeholders
Because estimating is a waste of time and should always be avoided
Because the Product Owner has not finished writing all requirements yet
Because the work is complex and much will only be learned by building, so a probabilistic range updated every Sprint is more honest and more useful than a false precise date
explanation: Complexity means that unknowns are discovered through doing, so ranges refined by real delivery data serve decision-making better than a precise but unfounded date. Scrum encourages transparency with stakeholders about dates and risk. Estimation is not banned; over-reliance on it is the problem.

question: Which is a valid reason to cancel a Sprint?
options: The Sprint Goal becomes obsolete
The Developers will not finish all forecasted Product Backlog items
A key Developer is unexpectedly absent
Velocity is lower than the Sprint before
explanation: A Sprint may be cancelled only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, and only the Product Owner has the authority to do so. Unfinished items, absences or lower output are normal situations handled by re-planning within the Sprint. Cancelling a Sprint is traumatic and rare.

question: A company funds projects annually and disbands teams when a project ends. A Scrum Master wants to improve delivery capability. Which change should they advocate for most strongly?
options: Longer Sprints so that each project phase fits within one Sprint
More detailed annual estimates so that funding is more accurate
Stable, long-lived teams funded around products, so capability, domain knowledge and predictability accumulate instead of being destroyed
Assigning each Developer to several projects to maximize utilization
explanation: Scrum relies on stable Scrum Teams that improve over time; repeatedly disbanding them destroys learned capability and makes forecasting unreliable. High individual utilization across projects increases context switching and reduces flow. Longer Sprints and finer upfront estimates do not address the structural cause.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Scrum Team / Scrum Master

question: Which statements correctly distinguish output from outcome when measuring a product? (Choose two.)
options: Reduction in customer time to complete a key task is an outcome measure
Lines of code written per Developer indicates product value
Number of features released in a quarter is an output measure
Outcome measures are only relevant to the Scrum Master
Story points completed per Sprint is the best proxy for customer value
explanation: Outputs describe what was produced, such as feature counts, while outcomes describe the change experienced by users or the business, such as faster task completion. Story points and lines of code are effort or size proxies and say nothing about value. Outcome focus is primarily a Product Owner concern supported by the whole Scrum Team.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Owner / Evidence-Based Management

question: How does the Scrum Guide 2020 treat practices such as test-driven development, pair programming and continuous integration?
options: They are mandatory elements of the Developers' accountability
They are forbidden because Scrum is a framework, not a methodology
They are complementary practices outside Scrum that teams may adopt to improve technical quality and the ability to deliver a done Increment
They may only be used by teams working on software products with more than ten Developers
explanation: Scrum is deliberately incomplete and does not prescribe engineering practices; techniques like TDD, pair programming and CI/CD sit outside the framework but often help teams meet a strong Definition of Done. They are neither required nor forbidden, and nothing in Scrum limits them by team size.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Scrum Definition / complementary practices

question: A team cannot produce a done Increment each Sprint because regression testing takes two weeks manually. Which focus is most likely to help?
options: Investing Sprint capacity in test automation and continuous integration so verification happens continuously
Adding a dedicated testing Sprint after every three Sprints
Removing testing from the Definition of Done until automation exists
Hiring more manual testers and keeping the same process
explanation: Automating the regression suite and integrating continuously removes the structural barrier to finishing work inside the Sprint. Testing Sprints and a weakened Definition of Done simply hide undone work and accumulate risk. More manual testers scale the bottleneck rather than removing it.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Definition of Done / Increment

question: Which outcomes can continuous integration and automated testing support for a Scrum Team? (Choose two.)
options: Faster feedback on whether the Increment still works after each change
Greater confidence that work can be considered done within the Sprint
Removal of the need for a Sprint Retrospective
Guaranteed defect-free software
Elimination of the need for a Definition of Done
explanation: Continuous integration and automated tests shorten the feedback loop on quality and make it practical to finish work to the Definition of Done inside the Sprint. They do not replace the Definition of Done or the Retrospective, and no practice guarantees defect-free software.

question: The Product Owner pressures the Developers to skip refactoring so more features fit into the Sprint. What is the most appropriate Scrum Master action?
options: Support the Product Owner, since they decide what is built
Tell the Developers to refactor secretly without mentioning it
Help both sides see the trade-off, coaching that technical quality is part of being able to deliver value sustainably and that the Developers own how the work is done
Add a separate technical debt backlog owned by the Scrum Master
explanation: The Product Owner decides what is built and in what order, but the Developers decide how, including the quality work needed to keep the product changeable. Making the cost of accumulating technical debt transparent lets both make better decisions. A hidden backlog or hidden work breaks transparency.

question: How should technical debt reduction work typically be handled in Scrum?
options: Through a separate backlog invisible to stakeholders
By the Scrum Master, who schedules it between Sprints
Only during hardening Sprints before each release
Made transparent, for example as Product Backlog items or by being built into the Definition of Done, so trade-offs are visible and ordered
explanation: Everything that affects the product's value and the team's ability to deliver should be transparent, so quality work is either represented in the Product Backlog or prevented by a strong Definition of Done. Hidden backlogs defeat transparency, hardening Sprints defer quality, and a new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends.

question: Two Developers want to adopt pair programming; a manager objects that it halves productivity. What is the most useful Scrum Master contribution?
options: Mandate pair programming for the whole team
Agree with the manager and stop the experiment
Encourage the Developers to run it as an experiment and inspect the effect on quality, rework and knowledge sharing at the Retrospective
Escalate the manager's comment to senior leadership
explanation: The Developers decide their own working practices, and an empirical experiment inspected in the Retrospective settles the question with evidence rather than opinion. Mandating the practice removes self-management, and abandoning it on assertion alone ignores empiricism. Escalation is disproportionate.

question: Who decides which engineering practices a Scrum Team uses to build the Increment?
options: The Developers, who are accountable for creating a plan and for quality by adhering to the Definition of Done
The Scrum Master, as the process expert
The Product Owner, who owns the product
The organization's enterprise architects
explanation: The Developers are self-managing and decide how to turn Product Backlog items into an Increment, including technical practices, while adhering to the agreed Definition of Done. Neither the Scrum Master nor the Product Owner dictates technique, and organizational standards, if any, form part of the Definition of Done.

question: A team delivers an Increment every Sprint but each release to production requires three days of manual deployment steps. What is the best framing for the Scrum Master?
options: This is outside Scrum and therefore outside the Scrum Master's interest
The team should stop producing Increments until deployment is automated
This is an impediment to delivering value frequently; the Scrum Master should make its cost transparent and support investment in deployment automation
The Product Owner should simply release less often to reduce the cost
explanation: Anything that delays getting a usable Increment into users' hands constrains value and feedback, so it belongs squarely in the Scrum Master's impediment work with the team and organization. Deployment automation is a complementary practice but the delay it addresses is a Scrum concern. Releasing less often reduces feedback and increases batch risk.

question: Which facilitation behaviors help a Scrum Master run an effective Sprint Retrospective? (Choose three.)
options: Ensuring quieter team members have the opportunity to contribute
Inviting managers so team members can be held accountable for mistakes
Presenting a list of improvements they have decided the team must adopt
Using data such as defects, cycle time or incidents to ground the discussion
Creating a safe environment where difficult topics can be raised
explanation: Effective retrospective facilitation builds psychological safety, grounds discussion in evidence, and draws out all voices so the team itself identifies improvements. The Scrum Master facilitates rather than dictating improvements, and inviting managers to assign blame destroys the safety the event depends on.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Sprint Retrospective / Scrum Master

question: During a Retrospective, two Developers begin a personal argument that shuts down the discussion. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: End the Retrospective immediately and reschedule for next Sprint
Decide who is right so the team can move on
Intervene to re-establish respect, help both articulate their underlying concerns, and refocus the group on the team's system and improvements
Report both Developers to their line manager
explanation: Facilitating conflict means restoring a respectful environment and surfacing the real interests behind the positions so the team can address the issue productively. Deciding who is right removes the team's ownership, and ending the event abandons an improvement opportunity. Escalating to managers undermines trust and self-management.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Scrum Values / Sprint Retrospective

question: A Scrum Team's Retrospectives produce the same improvement items Sprint after Sprint without change. What is the most helpful action?
options: Stop holding Retrospectives since they are not working
Have the Scrum Master implement the improvements for the team
Help the team select one or two improvements, make them visible, and include at least one in the next Sprint Backlog so it actually gets done
Lengthen the Retrospective time-box to discuss more topics
explanation: Scrum suggests that the most impactful improvements be addressed as soon as possible, often by adding them to the next Sprint Backlog, which turns intentions into work that is actually done. Dropping the event or having the Scrum Master do everything removes team ownership. More discussion time without follow-through changes nothing.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Sprint Retrospective / Sprint Backlog

question: Which statement best describes the Scrum Master's facilitation of Scrum events?
options: The Scrum Master must chair and lead every event personally
The Scrum Master ensures events take place, are positive and productive, and kept within the time-box, while the team may facilitate them
The Scrum Master attends only the Sprint Retrospective
The Scrum Master decides the outcome of each event
explanation: The Scrum Master ensures that all events happen and are positive, productive and within their time-boxes, but does not need to run each one or dictate outcomes. Mature teams often facilitate their own events. Outcomes belong to the accountable people and the team.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Scrum Master / Scrum Events

question: Sprint Planning regularly runs far over its time-box because the items are poorly understood. What should the Scrum Master encourage?
options: Removing the time-box for Sprint Planning
Continuous Product Backlog refinement during the Sprint so items are sufficiently understood before Sprint Planning
Letting the Product Owner plan the Sprint alone and inform the Developers
Introducing a Sprint Zero to refine the entire backlog
explanation: Refinement is an ongoing activity that adds detail and order to Product Backlog items so Sprint Planning can be efficient and focused. Time-boxes are fixed maximums in Scrum and are not removed. Planning without the Developers removes their accountability, and Sprint Zero is an anti-pattern.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Backlog refinement / Sprint Planning

question: A Scrum Team works across three time zones. Which actions best support Scrum's empirical foundations? (Choose two.)
options: Having each location hold its own Sprint Review with local stakeholders only
Allowing each location to define its own Definition of Done
Agreeing on overlapping working hours so the Developers can hold the Daily Scrum and collaborate
Keeping artifacts and the Increment radically transparent in tools accessible to everyone
Replacing all events with asynchronous written status updates
explanation: Distributed teams still need real collaboration and a single shared view of reality, so overlapping hours for events and highly transparent shared artifacts are key enablers. Replacing events with status updates removes inspection and adaptation, and local Sprint Reviews or local Definitions of Done fragment transparency and quality.

question: A fully remote Scrum Team reports that Daily Scrums have become a round of status reports to the Scrum Master. What is the best intervention?
options: Cancel the Daily Scrum since remote teams communicate in chat anyway
Have the Scrum Master ask each person three questions in a fixed order
Coach the Developers to own the event, focusing on progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapting their plan, and consider the Scrum Master stepping back from attending
Require cameras on and extend the event to 30 minutes
explanation: The Daily Scrum is the Developers' event for inspecting progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapting the Sprint Backlog; when it becomes reporting to the Scrum Master, stepping back restores ownership. The Scrum Master participates as a peer only if actively working on Sprint Backlog items. Scripted questions and longer time-boxes do not change the dynamic.

question: A distributed Scrum Team has Developers in one country and the Product Owner in another, with questions answered after a 24-hour delay. What is the most significant consequence?
options: The Sprint length must be increased to eight weeks
Decisions and clarifications are delayed, reducing the team's ability to adapt within the Sprint and risking the Sprint Goal
The Developers must choose a local proxy Product Owner to decide on backlog items
The Definition of Done must be weakened to accommodate the delay
explanation: Slow feedback from the Product Owner undermines daily adaptation and jeopardizes the Sprint Goal, which is why availability matters more than location. A proxy who makes decisions splits the Product Owner accountability. Longer Sprints and weaker quality standards treat the symptom and make empiricism worse.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Owner / Sprint Goal

question: Which approach best helps a Scrum Master resolve a disagreement between the Product Owner and the Developers about whether an item is done?
options: Letting the Product Owner decide case by case what counts as done
Referring to the shared Definition of Done and, if it is ambiguous, facilitating the team to clarify it for future Sprints
Asking stakeholders to vote at the Sprint Review
Marking the item done and tracking the remainder as a defect
explanation: The Definition of Done provides the shared, transparent standard for when work is complete, so disputes are resolved by applying it and improving it where unclear. Ad hoc decisions or stakeholder votes destroy the consistency the Definition of Done exists to provide. Reclassifying unfinished work as a defect hides reality.

question: Which Scrum Value most directly supports team members raising uncomfortable problems during a Retrospective?
options: Focus
Courage
Commitment
Respect
explanation: Courage is what enables Scrum Team members to do the right thing and work on tough problems, including naming difficult issues despite discomfort. Respect and Focus support how the team works together and where attention goes. Commitment concerns dedication to the goals of the Scrum Team.

question: Which situations indicate that a Scrum Master should coach rather than directly solve a problem? (Choose two.)
options: A required third-party licence has expired and must be purchased
A building access badge for a new Developer has not been issued
A server outage is blocking all builds and needs a vendor call
The Developers are unsure how to split a large Product Backlog item
The team repeatedly avoids discussing a recurring quality problem
explanation: Coaching builds the team's own capability, which is appropriate for skills such as splitting work and for team behaviors such as avoiding a difficult topic. Administrative or external obstacles like badges, licences and vendor outages are usually best removed directly or by engaging the right people so the Developers can keep working.

question: A Scrum Master facilitates a session where stakeholders with conflicting priorities must be heard before the Product Owner decides. What is the most appropriate facilitation goal?
options: Reaching unanimous agreement among all stakeholders before proceeding
Ensuring each perspective and its underlying need is understood and transparent so the Product Owner can make an informed, accountable decision
Having the group vote, with the majority determining backlog order
Letting the Scrum Master determine the ordering based on what is fairest
explanation: Facilitation aims to surface information and understanding; the Product Owner remains the single person accountable for Product Backlog ordering. Demanding unanimity stalls decisions, and voting or Scrum Master ordering transfers accountability away from the Product Owner.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Owner / Scrum Master

question: A remote team's Sprint Review consists of a slide deck describing what was built. What should the Scrum Master suggest?
options: Demonstrating the working Increment itself and inviting stakeholders to use it, then discussing what to do next
Pre-recording the slides to save time in the event
Replacing the Sprint Review with a written release note
Having only the Product Owner attend to represent the team
explanation: The Sprint Review exists to inspect the actual outcome of the Sprint and adapt the Product Backlog, which requires real working functionality rather than descriptions. Slides, recordings or release notes provide no reliable basis for inspection. The Scrum Team and stakeholders collaborate together in the event.

question: A newly formed distributed Scrum Team wants to spend the first two Sprints setting up tooling and architecture with no usable functionality. How should the Scrum Master respond?
options: Approve it as a necessary Sprint Zero
Encourage them to deliver a thin end-to-end slice of real functionality in the first Sprint, building just enough infrastructure to support it
Tell them Scrum forbids any infrastructure work
Suggest they skip Sprint Reviews until functionality exists
explanation: Every Sprint must produce a usable Increment, so infrastructure is built incrementally in service of a real slice of functionality rather than as a separate preparatory phase. Scrum does not forbid infrastructure work, it forbids Sprints that produce no value. Skipping Sprint Reviews removes an essential inspection point.

question: Does Scrum require Scrum Team members to be located in the same physical office?
options: Yes, co-location is mandatory in Scrum
No, but the team must still collaborate closely and hold all Scrum events, which is harder when distributed
Yes, except for the Product Owner
No, and distribution has no effect on the team's effectiveness
explanation: Scrum does not prescribe location; it requires a cohesive, collaborative team that holds its events and produces a done Increment each Sprint. Distribution is permitted but adds communication challenges that the team must deliberately address. Pretending distribution is cost-free ignores real coordination effort.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Scrum Team / Scrum Events

question: Which conditions make it easier for a Scrum Team to deliver a done Increment every Sprint? (Choose three.)
options: A dedicated stabilization phase after every release
Product Backlog items sliced small enough to be finished within a Sprint
Automated build, test and deployment pipelines
Separate teams for development and testing with formal handoffs
A clear, shared Definition of Done that includes all quality work
explanation: A strong Definition of Done, automation that gives fast quality feedback, and small, finishable items all directly enable finishing work inside the Sprint. Separate testing teams introduce handoffs and queues, while stabilization phases move quality work outside the Sprint, both of which prevent a truly done Increment.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Definition of Done / Increment

question: A Scrum Master observes that the Developers never challenge the Product Owner's decisions even when they foresee technical problems. What is the deepest concern?
options: The Product Owner is exceeding their authority by ordering the Product Backlog
The team lacks the safety and courage needed for transparency, so risks stay hidden and inspection is based on incomplete information
The Developers should be formally allowed to veto Product Backlog items
The Scrum Master should start attending all Product Owner meetings as an observer
explanation: Empiricism depends on transparency, and silence about foreseen risks means decisions are made on incomplete information; fostering courage and respect is core Scrum Master work. Ordering the Product Backlog is legitimately the Product Owner's accountability, so a formal veto is not the answer. Surveillance of meetings does not build safety.

question: Which situation is an example of the 'Scrum Master as secretary' anti-pattern?
options: The Scrum Master coaches the Developers on splitting Product Backlog items
The Scrum Master updates the task board and writes meeting notes on behalf of the Developers every day
The Scrum Master helps the Product Owner find techniques for Product Backlog ordering
The Scrum Master works with leadership to remove an organizational impediment
explanation: Doing the Developers' administrative work removes their ownership of the Sprint Backlog and consumes the Scrum Master's capacity for coaching and organizational change. Coaching the Developers, helping the Product Owner and working with leadership are genuine expressions of the accountability.

question: An organization measures its Scrum adoption by counting how many teams hold all the Scrum events. What is the main weakness of this measure?
options: It measures process compliance rather than the outcomes Scrum is meant to produce, such as value delivered and faster feedback
It is impossible to count events accurately
Scrum events are optional, so counting them is meaningless
Only the Scrum Master is allowed to measure adoption
explanation: Holding events is necessary but not sufficient; the purpose of Scrum is to deliver value through empiricism, so adoption is better judged by outcomes like delivery frequency, quality and customer impact. The Scrum events are required elements of the framework, not optional, so dismissing them is also wrong.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Scrum Events / Evidence-Based Management

question: Leadership asks which measures would tell them whether their product investment is paying off. Which combination best reflects evidence-based management thinking?
options: Velocity, utilization and number of Sprints completed
Current value delivered to customers, the organization's ability to innovate, time to market, and unrealized value still available in the market
Defect counts and number of Product Backlog items refined per Sprint
Headcount per team and average story size
explanation: Evidence-based management looks at value realized now, value still unrealized in the market, the speed of delivering new value, and the organization's capacity to innovate. Velocity, utilization, refinement counts and headcount describe activity or capacity, not value or market impact.

question: A Scrum Team completes many Product Backlog items each Sprint, but customer satisfaction is falling. Which conclusion is most sound?
options: The team should increase the number of items completed per Sprint
High output is not the same as valuable outcomes; the Product Owner should seek customer feedback and adapt the Product Backlog and Product Goal
The Definition of Done is too strict and should be relaxed
The Sprint length should be shortened so more items are completed
explanation: Producing more features that customers do not value simply increases waste; the response is to inspect outcomes and adapt what is built. Weakening quality standards or compressing Sprints to boost throughput addresses the wrong variable. Output volume is not evidence of value.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Owner / Product Goal

question: Three months into an adoption, teams follow the events but managers still assign work to individuals and approve designs. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: The teams are practising Scrum correctly, since all events occur
The organization has adopted the mechanics without the self-management Scrum depends on, so the benefits of empiricism will not materialize
Scrum does not apply to organizations with managers
The Scrum Master should take over work assignment from the managers
explanation: Scrum Teams are self-managing and decide who does what and how, so external assignment and design approval hollow out the framework even when events are held. Scrum works in organizations with managers, but their role must shift to supporting rather than directing the work. The Scrum Master assigning work would repeat the same dysfunction.

question: Why is a 'hardening Sprint' before release considered an anti-pattern?
options: Because Sprints must all be the same length
Because the Product Owner cannot attend it
Because it means previous Increments were not actually done, hiding incomplete work and risk
Because it requires an additional Scrum Master
explanation: If stabilization and testing are needed after the fact, the earlier Increments did not meet the Definition of Done and transparency was false. The right response is to strengthen the Definition of Done and do the quality work inside each Sprint. The issue is undone work, not scheduling or staffing.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Definition of Done / Increment

question: Which behaviors suggest that a Product Owner has become a proxy rather than a true Product Owner? (Choose two.)
options: They engage directly with customers to validate assumptions
They say no to a stakeholder request after weighing it against the Product Goal
They relay requirements from a business manager without authority to change priorities
They must obtain approval before changing the Product Backlog order
They involve the Developers in Product Backlog refinement
explanation: A proxy passes messages and needs approval for decisions, which slows adaptation and breaks the single point of accountability for value. Declining requests, refining collaboratively with the Developers and talking to customers are all signs of a genuine Product Owner exercising their accountability.

question: A Scrum Master is asked to also act as the line manager who writes performance appraisals for the Developers. What is the main risk?
options: The Scrum Master would have too little time for facilitation
Scrum explicitly forbids a Scrum Master from having any other role in the company
Team members may stop being open about problems and mistakes, reducing transparency and the effectiveness of Retrospectives
The Product Owner would lose the authority to order the Product Backlog
explanation: Evaluative authority over team members chills openness, which is the foundation of inspection and honest Retrospectives. Scrum does not legislate HR structures, but the Scrum Master must consider how the combination affects safety and trust. Product Owner authority is unaffected.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Scrum Values / Scrum Master

question: A Scrum Master wants to start an organizational change toward Scrum but has no formal authority. Which approach is most likely to succeed?
options: Mandate Scrum practices and escalate non-compliance
Wait for an executive sponsor to drive the entire change
Start where there is willingness, make the results and remaining obstacles transparent, and use early evidence to build support more widely
Introduce the complete target operating model in one organization-wide launch
explanation: Change through influence works best by producing visible evidence of improvement in a willing area and using it to earn broader sponsorship, which matches empirical, incremental change. Mandates breed compliance without belief, waiting forfeits agency, and big-bang rollouts remove the ability to inspect and adapt the change itself.

question: Which statement about the Sprint Backlog is correct when management wants visibility into daily progress?
options: The Sprint Backlog belongs to the Developers, is highly visible, and is updated by them throughout the Sprint as more is learned
The Sprint Backlog must be approved by management before the Sprint starts
The Scrum Master maintains the Sprint Backlog for reporting purposes
The Sprint Backlog is private to the Developers and should not be visible to anyone else
explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work the Developers plan to do, owned and updated by them. Transparency means others can see it, but no one outside the Developers controls or approves it. The Scrum Master does not maintain it.

question: After a serious production incident, leadership asks the Scrum Master for a root-cause report naming responsible individuals. What is the best response?
options: Produce the report naming the Developers who made the changes
Decline to investigate because Scrum does not address incidents
Propose a blameless examination of the system and process that allowed the defect to reach production, and work with the team on concrete improvements
Tell leadership the Product Owner is solely accountable for the incident
explanation: Scrum treats the Scrum Team as collectively accountable and improves through inspecting the process, so a blameless systemic analysis produces real improvement while naming individuals destroys safety and transparency. Refusing to engage ignores a genuine organizational concern. Singling out the Product Owner misassigns accountability for quality.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Scrum Team / Sprint Retrospective

question: What does it mean that the Scrum Team is cross-functional?
options: Every member can do every task equally well
The members collectively have all the skills needed to create value each Sprint
The team contains at least one person from each department
Team members rotate between teams every Sprint
explanation: Cross-functional means the team collectively possesses the skills required to create a valuable Increment without depending on others. It does not require identical skills in every member, departmental representation, or rotation, which would in fact harm team stability.

question: A Scrum Team is repeatedly pulled into unplanned production support, endangering Sprint Goals. What is the most constructive approach?
options: Ignore support requests until the Sprint ends
Make the volume and impact of support work transparent, agree with the Product Owner how it is accounted for when forecasting, and address the root causes of the defects
Have the Scrum Master handle all support requests personally
Stop setting a Sprint Goal so interruptions no longer matter
explanation: Transparency about interrupt work lets the Product Owner and Developers plan realistically, while reducing the defect source attacks the cause rather than the symptom. Ignoring real customer problems is not viable and the Scrum Master absorbing the work hides the issue. Every Sprint requires a Sprint Goal, which gives the team focus.

question: Which signals indicate that an organization's Scrum adoption is producing real benefits rather than cosmetic change? (Choose three.)
options: Every team reports a rising velocity trend
The number of documented processes has increased
Usable Increments reach real users more frequently than before
Teams decide how to do their work without external assignment
Decisions are increasingly based on observed outcomes rather than opinion
explanation: Frequent delivery to users, genuine self-management and decisions grounded in evidence are the behavioral changes that produce Scrum's benefits. Rising velocity is a team-relative, non-Scrum number that can be inflated, and more documentation is unrelated to value delivery.

question: The Developers want to stop using story points and instead forecast using the number of items completed per Sprint. How should the Scrum Master react?
options: Forbid it, because Scrum requires story point estimation
Support it as an experiment, since Scrum does not prescribe an estimation technique, as long as items still have a size and the team can plan and forecast
Require them to keep using story points for management reporting
Allow it only if the Product Owner stops asking about dates
explanation: Scrum requires Product Backlog items to have a size attribute determined by the Developers, but prescribes no technique; counting small, similarly sized items is a legitimate flow-based alternative. The Developers choose how they plan, so mandating a method for reporting convenience undermines self-management. Forecasting remains possible without points.

question: An organization wants one Scrum Master to serve twelve teams part-time to save cost. What is the most important point for the Scrum Master to make?
options: Scrum requires exactly one full-time Scrum Master per team
The Scrum Master should instead be made a line manager over the teams
At that ratio the Scrum Master can only act as an event organizer, not as a coach and change agent, so team effectiveness and the organizational improvements Scrum needs will not be achieved
Twelve teams are fine as long as each team has its own Product Owner
explanation: Scrum does not set a numeric ratio, but the Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness and for organizational change, which requires real presence and depth of engagement. Spread too thin, the accountability degrades into scheduling. Making the Scrum Master a manager would conflict with fostering self-management.

question: An organization requires a separate QA department to test each Increment for two weeks after the Sprint ends before anything can be released. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Accept it as an organizational constraint and plan a testing Sprint after every three Sprints
Work with the Scrum Team and the organization to fold the required testing into the Definition of Done so every Increment is usable at Sprint end
Ask the Product Owner to stop calling the output an Increment until QA has signed it off
Lengthen the Sprint to six weeks so the QA cycle fits inside it
explanation: An Increment must meet the Definition of Done and be usable when it is created, so externally mandated quality work belongs inside the Definition of Done and inside the Sprint. Hardening or testing Sprints, redefining the Increment, and stretching the Sprint to absorb a handoff all preserve the dysfunction instead of removing the impediment, which is exactly what the Scrum Master should help the organization change.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Increment / Definition of Done

question: Which actions by a Scrum Master support stakeholders during a Scrum adoption? (Choose two.)
options: Requiring stakeholders to submit all requests through a formal change control board
Attending all stakeholder meetings in place of the Product Owner
Promising stakeholders fixed scope on fixed dates to reduce anxiety
Removing barriers between stakeholders and the Scrum Team
Helping stakeholders understand empirical product planning and what they can expect from each Sprint
explanation: Scrum Masters serve the organization by coaching stakeholders in empirical approaches and by removing barriers between them and the Scrum Teams. False certainty and heavyweight change control recreate the problems Scrum addresses, and substituting for the Product Owner weakens that accountability.

question: A Scrum Team is asked to adopt a mandated organizational process that conflicts with its Definition of Done. How should the Scrum Master proceed?
options: Instruct the team to quietly ignore the mandated process
Have the team comply and accept the resulting undone work
Make the conflict and its consequences transparent to the people who own the process and work with them toward a resolution that preserves a releasable Increment
Ask the Product Owner to approve lowering the Definition of Done
explanation: Conflicts between organizational standards and the ability to produce a done Increment are impediments to be surfaced and resolved with the owners of the process. Silent non-compliance breaks transparency, while accepting undone work or lowering quality standards creates hidden risk. Where organizational standards exist, the Definition of Done must meet or exceed them rather than contradict them.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Definition of Done / Scrum Master

question: During Sprint Planning the Developers realize a critical dependency on another team will not be resolved this Sprint. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Plan the work anyway and hope the dependency clears
Craft a Sprint Goal and select work that can be completed without the dependency, make the impediment transparent, and have the Scrum Master help resolve it
Cancel the Sprint before it starts
Ask the Product Owner to order the dependent item lower permanently
explanation: Sprint Planning should produce a feasible Sprint Goal and a realistic plan, so the team selects work it can actually complete while the blocking dependency is made visible and pursued. Planning on hope endangers the Sprint Goal. Permanently deprioritizing valuable work or cancelling the Sprint avoids rather than resolves the impediment.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Sprint Planning / Scrum Master

question: A large programme replaces its phase gates with Sprint Reviews, but each Review still ends with a formal go/no-go decision by a governance board that overrules the Product Owner. What is the most significant issue?
options: The Sprint Review is being held too frequently
The Product Owner's decisions are not respected, so the single point of accountability for value is undermined and adaptation slows
Governance boards may never see an Increment
The Sprint Review should not include stakeholders at all
explanation: Scrum requires the whole organization to respect the Product Owner's decisions; a board overruling them reinstates the gate culture that blocks rapid adaptation. Stakeholders, including governance representatives, are welcome at the Sprint Review to inspect and collaborate. The frequency of Reviews is set by the Sprint cadence and is not the problem.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Product Owner / Sprint Review

question: Two Scrum Teams repeatedly build conflicting implementations of the same capability. Which response fits Scrum best?
options: Appoint a lead architect to approve all designs before coding
Have the Product Owner assign exclusive ownership of code areas to each team
Facilitate direct collaboration between the Developers of both teams, including shared standards in the Definition of Done and frequent integration to reveal conflicts early
Merge the two teams into one team of eighteen Developers
explanation: Self-managing Developers coordinate directly, and shared standards plus continuous integration expose conflicts while they are cheap to resolve. Design approval by an architect creates a bottleneck and reduces team accountability, and code ownership boundaries create component silos. A team of eighteen exceeds the guidance of typically ten or fewer people.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Developers / Definition of Done

question: What is the purpose of the Sprint Goal when stakeholders request changes mid-Sprint?
options: It prevents any discussion with stakeholders during the Sprint
It creates coherence and focus, and scope may be renegotiated with the Product Owner as long as the Sprint Goal is not endangered
It locks the Sprint Backlog so no changes are possible
It allows the Developers to refuse all feedback until the Sprint Review
explanation: The Sprint Goal gives the Developers flexibility in how they work while keeping them focused on a single objective; scope can be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner without endangering the Goal. It neither freezes the Sprint Backlog nor forbids collaboration or feedback.

question: An organization running eight teams on one product wants to improve its ability to release. Which changes most directly address that goal? (Choose two.)
options: Integrating all teams' work continuously so an integrated Increment exists at least every Sprint
Strengthening the shared Definition of Done so that releasable means releasable for all teams
Introducing a weekly cross-team status meeting for managers
Having each team report velocity to a central dashboard
Creating a separate release management team that owns final testing
explanation: Continuous integration across teams and a shared, strong Definition of Done are what make a genuinely releasable product Increment possible at any time. Status meetings and velocity dashboards add reporting without changing delivery capability, and a separate release team reintroduces handoffs and undone work.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Increment / Definition of Done

question: A Scrum Master has removed the same impediment for a team three Sprints in a row. What should they most likely do next?
options: Continue removing it each Sprint as part of their service to the team
Treat the recurrence as a signal of a systemic cause, help the team make it transparent and address the underlying condition, building the team's capability to handle it
Add the impediment to the Product Backlog so the Product Owner can order it
Accept it as a normal cost of working in a large organization
explanation: A recurring impediment indicates a systemic cause, and the Scrum Master's deeper service is to change the system and grow the team's ability to deal with such issues rather than repeatedly applying the same fix. Impediments are not Product Backlog items for the Product Owner to order. Accepting the waste abandons the improvement accountability.
reference: Scrum Guide 2020 - Scrum Master / Sprint Retrospective
